cells.tense: You are here, with your hands on it, and the keeping-alive is going well.
cells.act: do the giving in the open this time, where it was always done unseen
cells.ask: Carry one piece of the work where it can be seen — whatever repair you usually make out of sight. Whoever it's for gets to be there while you do it. Offer no reason for the change.
cells.core:
Two things need you and you're holding both, and what's in your care gets fed instead of forced. This is the shape of it when it's going well: nothing has to be dropped, and you're not braced for the next thing to go wrong. What goes unsaid is how much of it runs on what you've quietly taken on.

Next time you do the piece nobody sees, do it where the one it's for can watch. Not a speech — just the work, visible, once. When a thank-you comes, stay long enough to hear it through. You're good at the doing and bad at the receiving, and the second one is where all the weight you're carrying would actually get set down.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it alive. Let someone watch you at it.

cells.tense: You will be braced for something further out that has not arrived yet.
cells.act: let the satisfaction of a finished thing land
cells.ask: Something you tend is already through — done, standing. Give it an hour as it is: no improving, no starting the next. Sit with what got finished and leave it alone.
cells.core:
Where you tend what's in your care, the work runs a season ahead of what's actually here. Two demands are held, and held well, and keeping them level has come to feel like standing on ground that might give. So the next thing gets planted before the last one can be looked at. What you're growing is real; it's that the crop you're standing in is the one that isn't up yet.

One of the things you've already finished is finished. Give it an hour with nothing done to it — no improving, no planning the next. If sitting with it is hard, that's the part of this you haven't trained, and the not-sitting is what makes all of it heavier than the work itself.
cells.sheetLine: What you tend is fine. Go stand in what it made.

cells.tense: You were tending something once, and you are still standing where it came apart.
cells.act: go on toward it without needing a sign
cells.ask: Go on toward what you chose before it went quiet. Take an ordinary step this week and don't go looking for anything coming back. No proof, no signal. The step itself is the whole of it.
cells.core:
A structure you were carrying came apart, and it came apart honestly — it wasn't holding anything real. What's in you to tend hasn't gone anywhere; that isn't what stopped. What stopped was the part where you could see it working. So you're standing at the place where it fell, waiting to be shown the work is still worth it.

Keep going toward the thing you'd already chosen, without waiting for it to show you anything. One small, ordinary act, and no checking for a response. The sign you're waiting on isn't late; it was going to come from somewhere else. What you decided still stands, and it can carry a week of not-knowing without any help.
cells.sheetLine: The thing you chose still stands. Go on toward it.

cells.tense: You are already keeping it standing, and no one — including you — would say so.
cells.act: stand where the giving can be witnessed
cells.ask: Carry the load-bearing part for someone here, next time, where they can watch. No speech and no ask for credit. Visible once, with nothing said about what it costs.
cells.core:
The thing is being kept standing. Two demands are held level, the load-bearing part is carried, and if anyone asked, you'd describe yourself as outside of it. The room stopped buying that some time ago — they can see who's holding it up. What hasn't caught up is your own account: the one doing the work doesn't get counted among the ones keeping this alive, not even by themselves.

Do the next load-bearing bit where it can be seen. No speech, no bid for credit — the visible act, once, with nothing said about what it takes out of you. Take the thank-you if it comes. The structure belonged to more than them. No lid was going to fit over a thing this size.

attempts.check: The record never says this person tends land, money or a patch of earth; the seat they drew is an inner one, so my read of what they steward has to stay in what they carry rather than what they hold, and a listener could fairly say I've made the tending material when the draw says inner. The asks survive that being wrong: each one is doable by someone who tends people, work or a household, and each teaches something about where the giving shows. The sentence that serves me more than them is the closing image of the lid not fitting — it's the prettiest line in the quartet and I'm keeping it only because it says something true about a structure that couldn't hold.
